content: For anatoxin-a variants, while the available data were insufficient to establish a definitive guideline value, a provisional reference value was determined. Quantitative reference standards are required for congeners. For further details, refer to Chapter 12 fact sheets. The detection limit for certain substances lies between the guideline value and one-tenth of its value. In other cases, the detection limit ranges between one-tenth and one-fiftieth of the guideline value, and in some instances, it is below one-hundredth of the guideline value. Analytical methods are available to detect concentrations at the guideline value, but detecting concentrations as low as one-tenth of the guideline value can be challenging. A specific method involves the conversion of substances to their hydrides using a hydride generator. Chlorination can be achieved using liquefied chlorine gas, sodium hypochlorite solution, calcium hypochlorite granules, or on-site chlorine generators. Liquefied chlorine gas is supplied in pressurized containers, withdrawn from the cylinder, and dosed into water using a chlorinator, which controls and measures the gas flow rate. Sodium hypochlorite solution is dosed using a positive-displacement electric dosing pump or a gravity feed system. Calcium hypochlorite must be dissolved in water before being mixed with the main water supply. Chlorine, in any form, dissolves in water to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hypochlorite ion (OCl−). Various chlorination techniques include breakpoint chlorination, marginal chlorination, and superchlorination/dechlorination. Breakpoint chlorination involves dosing chlorine sufficiently to oxidize all ammonia nitrogen in the water and leave a residual free chlorine level to protect against reinfection. Superchlorination/dechlorination involves adding a large chlorine dose for rapid disinfection and chemical reaction, followed by reducing excess free chlorine to prevent taste issues. This method is used when bacterial loads are variable or detention time in a tank is insufficient. Marginal chlorination is used for high-quality water supplies, where chlorine is dosed to achieve a desired free residual chlorine level. Chlorine demand in such supplies is low, and a breakpoint may not occur. Chlorination is primarily employed for microbial disinfection. A disadvantage of chlorine is its reaction with natural organic matter, producing trihalomethanes and other halogenated disinfection by-products. However, optimizing the treatment system can control by-product formation. Ozonation is a powerful oxidation process used in water treatment, including the oxidation of organic chemicals. Ozone gas (O3) is generated by passing dry air or oxygen through a high-voltage electric field. The ozone-enriched air is dosed into water using porous diffusers at the base of baffled contactor tanks, which provide 10–20 minutes of contact time. At least 80% of the applied ozone should dissolve, with the remainder contained in off-gas, which is treated in an ozone destructor before venting. Ozonation performance depends on achieving the desired concentration after a given contact period, typically 5 mg/L after up to 20 minutes. Required doses vary with water type but are generally 2–5 mg/L. Higher doses are needed for untreated waters due to the ozone demand of natural organic matter. Ozone increases the biodegradability of natural organics, measured as assimilable organic carbon. To prevent bacterial growth in distribution systems, ozonation is often followed by biological filtration or granular activated carbon (GAC) treatment to remove biodegradable organics, and a chlorine residual is maintained since ozone does not provide a disinfectant residual. Ozone is effective for degrading a wide range of pesticides and organic chemicals. Other disinfection methods include chloramination, chlorine dioxide, UV radiation, and alternative techniques for small-scale applications, such as household water treatment. Chloramines (monochloramine, dichloramine, and trichloramine) are produced by reacting aqueous chlorine with ammonia. Monochloramine is the only useful chloramine disinfectant, and conditions are optimized to produce it exclusively. Monochloramine is less effective than free chlorine but is persistent, making it suitable as a secondary disinfectant for maintaining a stable residual in distribution systems. Chlorine dioxide has gained popularity due to concerns about disinfection by-products from chlorine. It is typically generated on-site by adding chlorine gas or solution to aqueous sodium chlorite. Chlorine dioxide decomposes in water to form chlorite and chlorate. UV radiation, emitted by lowor medium-pressure mercury arc lamps, is biocidal at wavelengths between 180 and 320 nm. It can inactivate protozoa, bacteria, bacteriophage, yeast, viruses, fungi, and algae. Turbidity can inhibit UV disinfection. UV radiation can also act as a catalyst in oxidation reactions when combined with ozone or hydrogen peroxide. Emerging disinfection techniques, such as bromine and iodine, show promise for expanded use. Bromine and iodine are halogens with biocidal properties. Iodine is commonly used for short-term applications, such as by travelers in areas with questionable water quality. Some forms of silver may have applications as bacteriostats or slow-acting disinfectants, but peer-reviewed data on their efficacy and risks are limited. Further analysis is needed to evaluate their biocidal efficacy, potential disinfection by-products, and risks from long-term exposure. Filtration processes remove particulate matter from raw water using rapid gravity, horizontal, pressure, or slow sand filters. Slow sand filtration is a biological process, while the others are physical treatment processes. Rapid gravity and pressure filters are commonly used for water pretreated by coagulation and sedimentation. Direct filtration involves adding coagulants to water, which then passes directly onto the filter, where precipitated floc and contaminants are removed. Dual-media or multimedia filters, incorporating materials of varying densities, allow efficient use of the entire bed depth for particle retention, reducing head loss development and enabling higher flow rates. Roughing filters, using coarse gravel or crushed stones, can treat high-turbidity water and are often used as pre-filters before slow sand filters. Bank filtration involves the natural filtration of surface water through groundwater via riverbed and banks, typically achieved by abstraction from boreholes near the surface water source. This low-cost method removes particulates and microorganisms, with sediments acting as filters and biofilters. Bank filtration can remove particles, bacteria, viruses, parasites, heavy metals, and biodegradable compounds. However, its performance depends on soil and geological conditions and source water quality. Site-specific testing is necessary to determine its feasibility and operational parameters. Aeration processes remove gases and volatile compounds through air stripping, achieved using cascades or air diffusion into water. Cascade aerators allow water to flow in thin films for efficient mass transfer but may introduce significant head loss. Compressed air can also be diffused through submerged perforated pipes. Aeration is used for oxidizing and precipitating iron and manganese, as well as removing volatile organic compounds, tasteand odor-causing compounds, and radon. Cascade aeration in packed towers is common, where water flows in thin films over plastic media with counter-current air flow. Aeration can increase water's dissolved oxygen content, potentially increasing its corrosivity toward metallic materials in distribution systems, which should be considered during treatment design. Chemical coagulation is the most common approach for treating surface waters, involving the addition of aluminum or iron salts to raw water under controlled conditions to form a solid flocculent metal hydroxide. Typical coagulant doses are 2–5 mg/L as aluminum or 4–10 mg/L as iron.
